questions.q: What actually produces useful evaluations and interpretations, according to the book?
options: Only skilled analysis and examination, which take training and practice
Reading as many opinions as possible
questions.explain: Untrained everyday thinking is vulnerable to error; skill comes from practice.
questions.evidence: Only skilled analysis and examinations will actually produce useful evaluations and interpretations

questions.q: Who should study critical thinking?
questions.explain: If your thinking affects you — and it affects everyone — you benefit from thinking better.
questions.evidence: The short answer to the question of who should study critical thinking is ‘Anyone who thinks.’.

questions.q: What is one of the most important steps when assessing or discussing ideas?
options: Deciding who is right before the discussion
Finding as many sources as possible
Settling on definitions for the key terms or concepts
questions.explain: Many disagreements disappear once terms are defined the same way.
questions.evidence: One of the most important steps in assessing or discussing ideas is to settle on definitions for the key terms or concepts.

questions.q: Formal logic is also known as…
questions.explain: Deductive arguments include syllogisms.
questions.evidence: Formal logic is known as deductive logic

questions.q: What does it mean for scientific claims to be 'reliable'?
options: They come from a famous scientist
They are popular on social media
They are backed by varied, repeatable evidence and can generate new predictions
questions.explain: Reliability is about the quality and repeatability of the evidence.
questions.evidence: Reliable means the claims are backed up by a variety of evidence, that the evidence is repeatable, and can be used to generate new predictions about the world.

questions.q: When is scepticism especially necessary?
options: For ideas and information that are immediately appealing to you
Only for claims made by strangers
questions.explain: We scrutinise what we dislike and wave through what we like.
questions.evidence: Scepticism is especially necessary for ideas and information that are immediately appealing to you.

questions.q: Why are the strongest valid deductive arguments called 'truth-preserving'?
options: Because the truth of the premises guarantees the truth of the conclusion
questions.explain: In a valid deductive argument, true premises cannot lead to a false conclusion.
questions.evidence: the truth of the premise guarantees or forces the truth of the conclusion.

questions.q: In a categorical syllogism, what is the first premise called?
questions.explain: The second premise is the minor premise.
questions.evidence: The first premise is called the major premise

questions.q: In an 'if… then…' (conditional) proposition, what is the 'if' part called?
questions.explain: The 'then' part is the consequent; modus ponens affirms the antecedent.
questions.evidence: the ‘if’ part is called the antecedent

questions.q: What are informal fallacies?
options: Mistakes where the reason offered is insufficient, irrelevant or ambiguous in supporting the conclusion
questions.explain: They are dangerous because they often look like good reasons.
questions.evidence: Informal fallacies are mistakes in reasoning that occur because the premise offered is insufficient, irrelevant, or ambiguous in its task of supporting the conclusion.

questions.q: Which phrase should alert you to a possible false dichotomy?
options: 'The alternative' — there is almost never a single alternative
questions.explain: Presenting only two options hides the others.
questions.evidence: Look out for key words such as the phrase ‘the alternative’, as there is almost never a single alternative.

questions.q: What is the 'backfire effect'?
options: Arguments that hurt the person making them
Showing people evidence against their beliefs can make them even more committed to those beliefs
questions.explain: Changing minds takes more than presenting facts.
questions.evidence: sometimes showing people new evidence and reasoning against their beliefs actually causes them to become even more committed to them.

questions.q: What is the questioning approach to learning called?
questions.explain: Asking questions drives your own thinking and stimulates the thinking of others.
questions.evidence: This questioning approach to learning is what is called the ‘Socratic method’

questions.q: How does questioning help the people who hear or answer your questions?
options: It makes them doubt everything they know
It shows who the expert in the room is
It stimulates new ideas and nurtures creativity
questions.explain: Good questions boost everyone's thinking, not just the questioner's.
questions.evidence: because questioning stimulates new ideas and nurtures creativity

questions.q: What does the book suggest to avoid only hearing ideas you already agree with?
options: Read only sources you already trust
Expose yourself to input you aren't used to or even disagree with
questions.explain: Unfamiliar or opposing input breaks the echo chamber that limits creative thinking.
questions.evidence: The solution is to try to expose yourself to input you aren’t used to or even disagree with.

questions.q: Which warning from physicist Richard Feynman does the book quote?
options: We mustn't fool ourselves, because we are the easiest to fool
questions.explain: Critical thinking starts with checking your own beliefs.
questions.evidence: who acknowledges that we mustn’t fool ourselves, as we are the easiest to fool

questions.q: How does the book compare processed information with processed food?
options: It is just as bad for you mentally, and possibly more addictive
It is healthier because it has already been checked
It has no effect on how we think
It is only harmful to children
questions.explain: Most information we consume has been heavily processed, so it calls for sharp thinking skills.
questions.evidence: processed information is just as bad for you mentally as processed food is for you physically

questions.q: When one proposition is offered as support for another, what roles do they play?
options: The first is a hypothesis; the second a theory
The first is a cause; the second an effect
The first is an inference; the second a fallacy
The supporting one is a premise; the supported one is a conclusion
questions.explain: The link between premises and conclusion is called the inference.
questions.evidence: the first proposition is playing the role of a premise, and the second proposition is playing the role of a conclusion

questions.q: According to the book, what is the most common reason an argument is unsound?
questions.explain: A fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that undermines how the premises support the conclusion.
questions.evidence: The most common reason an argument is unsound is because it’s fallacious.

questions.q: What are formal fallacies about?
options: How the premises connect to the conclusion, whatever their content
questions.explain: They can be spotted even when the premises are abstract or nonsense, such as 'all Klemps are Plerbs'.
questions.evidence: formal fallacies are all about how the premises connect to the conclusion

questions.q: According to the review of language and meaning, for whom is a language meaningful?
options: Only for the community that agrees to adopt its symbols
Only for people who write dictionaries
For computers but not for people
questions.explain: Words are abstract, arbitrary symbols whose meaning depends on shared agreement.
questions.evidence: language is only meaningful to those who are part of the community or social group that agree to adopt the symbols proposed by that system

questions.q: Why does the book call scientific confirmation 'weak and dubious'?
options: Experiments are too expensive to repeat
It is deductively invalid: it affirms the consequent
questions.explain: A theory predicting an observation, and the observation occurring, does not prove the theory true.
questions.evidence: Confirmation is always weak and dubious because it’s deductively invalid.

questions.q: How should the conclusions of inductive arguments be held?
options: As certain, once the premises are true
With some scepticism, because they are inconclusive and fallible
questions.explain: Induction gives probable, not guaranteed, conclusions — and the probability is rarely stated.
questions.evidence: just inconclusive and fallible, and therefore, should always be held with some scepticism

questions.q: In argument analysis, what does 'content' refer to?
options: The inference connecting reason and claim
questions.explain: Informal fallacies come from mishandling content; formal fallacies from faulty structure.
questions.evidence: Content refers to what an argument is about

questions.q: Why are fallacies so pervasive, according to the book?
options: They often appear to be good reasons
questions.explain: The appearance of a good reason is an illusion, which is what makes fallacies persuasive.
questions.evidence: Part of the reason fallacies are so pernicious and pervasive is that they often appear to be good reasons

questions.q: How does the amphiboly fallacy differ from equivocation?
options: Amphiboly uses statistics; equivocation uses emotion
Amphiboly is formal; equivocation is informal
They are two names for the same fallacy
Amphiboly is ambiguity in a sentence or phrase; equivocation is in a single word
questions.explain: Both are fallacies of ambiguous reasons; they differ in scale.
questions.evidence: whereas the amphiboly fallacy is sentence- or phrase-sized

questions.q: How do you carry out the 'five whys' technique?
options: Ask five different people the same question once
List five solutions and vote on them
Ask why about a problem, then repeat four more times, building on each answer
Write five reasons why the problem doesn't matter
questions.explain: Each answer becomes the next question, drilling down to a root cause.
questions.evidence: Repeat this process another four times, building off of the previous response each time to drill down to a root cause.

questions.q: Which problem should you choose to investigate with five whys?
options: A commonly occurring problem or one the team has prioritised
questions.explain: Root-cause analysis is worth the effort for problems that matter most.
questions.evidence: This could be the most commonly occurring problem or a problem that has been prioritized by the team.

questions.q: According to Andrew Baker, what does critical thinking help us do?
options: Evaluate how accurate and truthful statements and information are
questions.explain: It means analysing a question or problem down to its most basic parts.
questions.evidence: is what helps us evaluate the accuracy and truthfulness of statements, claims, and information we read and hear

questions.q: According to Baker, what drives progress forward in solving problems?
questions.explain: Critical thinking roots out the nature of a problem; creative thinking moves its solution forward.
questions.evidence: it is creative thinking that drives progress forward when it comes to solving these problems

questions.q: How does Baker describe exceptional creative thinkers?
options: They copy the best existing solutions
They invent new solutions that don't rely on past or current ones
questions.explain: Creativity is about new approaches to existing problems.
questions.evidence: Exceptional creative thinkers are people that invent new solutions to existing problems that do not rely on past or current solutions.

questions.q: How can we sharpen our critical thinking skills, according to Baker?
questions.explain: Ask questions such as: what is the source of this information?
questions.evidence: It is only through purposeful, frequent, intentional questioning such as this that we can sharpen our critical thinking skills

questions.q: Where, according to Baker, is more critical thinking demanded than in everyday life?
questions.explain: Study requires evaluating information and analysing many issues in a critical way.
questions.evidence: The academic setting demands more of us in terms of critical thinking than everyday life.
